name: Lundayeh
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

Opening statement and penult-stressed residue p. 51; ngecekuh and provisional-status caveat p. 52; 3.4.1 'The problem' (Omar 1983, Blust 2006:315, boundary-tone alternative, Malay debate) pp. 52-53; 3.4.2.1 Table 3.6 p. 54 and conclusion p. 55; 3.4.2.2 clipping pp. 55-56; 3.4.2.3 rhyme and meter p. 56..
catalog_quote: Kemaloh Lun Bawang stress is not contrastive and appears, from the available data, to usually fall on a word’s final syllable. When a word is spoken in isolation or occurs at the end of an intonational phrase, this stress is quite pronounced, seemingly thanks to the amplifying effects of a strong boundary tone. Outside this context, the contrast between the penultimate and final syllables of a word is much less obvious, with fairly similar weight given to each and only a slight, though highly consistent, preference for the ultima. In words of more than two syllables, the antepenult is noticeably unstressed by comparison to both the penult and the ultima, a fact no doubt connected to the antepenultimate neutralization phenomenon described in §3.3.2. Though stress seems to be predominantly final, it is not uniformly so; a small number of words consistently display penultimate stress. Some such words include pelanuk ‘mouse-deer,’ buayeh ‘crocodile,’ and lematek ‘leech.’ A few other words, such as kereb ‘time, when,’ despite being very common, do not appear to have a consistent distinction between the penult and ultima at all. One word, ngecekuh ‘because,’ displayed a tendency to stress the antepenult ... With potential confounding factors such as lengthening of word-final vowels and boundary tones factored out, the reasonable conclusion to adopt, until further work can confirm or refute it, is that Lun Bawang has word-final stress.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is non-contrastive and falls on the final syllable of the word; the ultima-over-penult difference is small (about 4 dB, 60-80 ms) except phrase-finally, where a boundary tone makes final prominence strong; antepenults are clearly unstressed. Mortensen treats this as a provisional conclusion pending a proper study separating stress from intonation, and notes Blust 2006's older-speaker data leaned to the penult.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; the penult carries near-equal weight in non-final position (no separate secondary-stress statement).
new_statements.exceptions: A small set of words with consistent penultimate stress (pelanuk 'mouse-deer', buayeh 'crocodile', lematek 'leech'); kereb 'time, when' shows no consistent penult/ultima distinction; ngecekuh 'because' tends to stress the antepenult. Author cites Blust 2006:315 that older recordings were 'relatively even on both of the last two syllables, but with a preference for the penult', younger speakers preferring final; and the N. Sarawak areal pattern 'final stress in citation forms but penultimate stress in phrasal context', which he raises as an alternative (penult + boundary tone) interpretation before rejecting it on measured data.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, measured in connected speech (three recordings, ~15 min, >800 words) with IU-final words and open final syllables excluded; citation/isolation forms show the strongest final prominence. Supported by clipping to the final syllable (ebpa' > pa', elung > long, Tadem > Dem) and by final-syllable rhyme and iambic meter in oral poetry (App. A.2-A.4).
new_statements.identity_note: Mortensen 2021 describes the Kemaloh dialect of Lun Bawang/Lundayeh (fieldwork at Long Semadoh, upper Trusan River, Sarawak; Kemaloh is the Bible-translation standard and highland lingua franca), which is the reference variety of lund1271 [lnd]; no separate dialect glottocode. Blust's Lun Dayeh remarks (as quoted) concern Long Semadoh/Bario-area speakers of the same language and Kelabit (kela1258). Glottolog's Yang 2021 'Bawang Horpa' reference is a misattribution (Sino-Tibetan Horpa, not Lun Bawang).

new_statements.quote: 1. STRESS. In PKLD and all of its known descendants other than Sa'ban stress is penultimate. In Sa'ban, as just noted, it is generally final, but may be marginally phonemic, depending upon the interpretation of extrametrical schwa in the sequences -/ieC/ and -/ueC/. [p. 267] || Stress is normally final, but surface contrasts are found in the sequence /ueC/ ... Since stress is normally final it is simplest to leave the default case unmarked. However, in the sequence /ueC/ the schwa is extrametrical, and stress is normally penultimate. [p. 266, on Sa'ban] || 5.2.4. Type 4: Syncope of an unstressed vowel. One likely precondition for erosion from the left in Sa'ban was a shift from the PKLD pattern of penultimate word stress to final stress. [p. 288]

new_statements.rule_in_words: For Lun Dayeh (as one of the 'known descendants' of Proto-Kelabit-Lun Dayeh other than Sa'ban) Blust states that word stress is penultimate; only Sa'ban, treated as a divergent KLD dialect, has shifted to (generally) final stress, with marginal penult/final surface contrasts in -ieC/-ueC sequences where a secondary schwa is extrametrical. The statement about Lun Dayeh is a one-line comparative generalization; the paper's own phonological description (pp. 262-267) is of Sa'ban, not of Lun Dayeh. The Lun Dayeh variety Blust cites lexicostatistically is the Long Semado dialect of Lun Bawang (p. 254).
new_statements.exceptions: None for Lun Dayeh. For Sa'ban: default final stress, but penultimate in /ueC/, /ieC/ with extrametrical (historically secondary) schwa, contrasting with oxytone /uweC/ (e.g. /luek/ 'spoon' paroxytone vs /luwek/ 'chest' oxytone), so stress 'may be marginally phonemic' there.
new_statements.identity_note: Blust 2001 is a description of Sa'ban (a divergent Kelabit-Lun Dayeh variety, own ISO snb / Glottolog saba1265-type entry, not lund1271); its statement about Lun Dayeh stress is a comparative aside covering all non-Sa'ban KLD dialects (Lun Dayeh = Lun Bawang, exemplified by the Long Semado dialect, plus Kelabit dialects such as Bario and Tring). The catalog record rests on Mortensen 2021, which describes the Kemaloh dialect of Lun Bawang (Long Semadoh / Ba' Kelalan, Sarawak). Long Semado(h) is within the Kemaloh Lun Bawang area, so the two sources speak about essentially the same regional variety, three to five decades apart (Blust fieldwork 1971; Mortensen fieldwork 2018-2020).

readall_conflicts: Blust 2001 (p. 267) states flatly that in Proto-Kelabit-Lun Dayeh 'and all of its known descendants other than Sa'ban stress is penultimate', which places Lun Dayeh/Lun Bawang stress on the penult, whereas the catalog record (from Mortensen 2021, sec. 3.4, pp. 51-55) has non-contrastive stress usually on the FINAL syllable in Kemaloh Lun Bawang. The disagreement is real but graded rather than categorical: Blust's remark is a one-sentence comparative generalization in a paper whose descriptive object is Sa'ban (final stress), based on his 1971 notes which (per Blust 2006:315 as quoted by Mortensen) recorded stress as 'relatively even on both of the last two syllables, but with a preference for the penult'; Mortensen 2021, the only dedicated instrumental treatment of a Lun Bawang dialect, finds near-even penult/ultima weight with a slight but consistent preference for the ultima (strongly final phrase-finally under a boundary tone), a handful of lexically penultimate words, and explicitly discusses Blust's penultimate claim and the possibility of a generational shift or a citation-form/phrasal-context difference. The catalog's fixed: final syllable reading (Mortensen) remains the best-supported; Blust 2001 should be logged as a contradicting older source (penultimate) with the note that both authors describe the last two syllables as nearly even in prominence.
